title: Reading & Analysing an Unseen Poem
description: A step-by-step method for approaching any unseen poem with confidence in the exam.
content_html:
What Is the Unseen Poetry Section?

Section C of AQA English Literature Paper 2 tests your ability to analyse poetry you have never seen before. Unlike the anthology section, you cannot prepare specific quotations or contextual knowledge. Instead, you must demonstrate your skills as a reader: your ability to identify what a poem is about, analyse how the poet creates meaning through language, structure, and form, and respond to the poem with your own interpretation.

Key Fact

Section C contains two questions. Question 27 asks you to analyse a single unseen poem and is worth 24 marks. Question 28 asks you to compare the first poem with a second unseen poem and is worth 8 marks. You should spend approximately 25 minutes on Q27 and 20 minutes on Q28.

Step 1: Read the Poem Three Times

The single most important thing you can do is read the poem carefully. Many students rush into writing and miss the poem’s meaning entirely. Use the first three minutes to read the poem three times:

First read: Get a general sense of the subject, tone, and mood. What is the poem about on the surface? Who is speaking? What is the situation?

Second read: Look for themes beneath the surface. What deeper ideas is the poet exploring? What feelings does the poem create? Note any shifts in tone or direction.

Third read: Begin annotating. Circle key words, underline striking images, note any techniques you recognise. Pay special attention to the opening and closing lines — they often contain the poem’s most important ideas.

Language: Powerful individual words (especially verbs and adjectives), imagery (metaphors, similes, personification), sound devices (alliteration, sibilance, onomatopoeia), semantic fields (groups of related words).

Structure: How the poem is organised. Does the mood shift? Is there a turning point (volta)? Does the poem build towards a climax or fade away? How does the ending relate to the beginning?

Form: The overall shape of the poem. Is it a sonnet? Free verse? Regular stanzas? Does it rhyme? What effect do the poet’s choices about line length, stanza breaks, and rhythm create?

Step 2: Identify the Poem’s Message

Before you write, summarise the poem’s message in one sentence. This keeps your response focused. For example: “The poet presents memory as something beautiful but painful, using natural imagery to show how the past fades over time.” Every paragraph you write should connect back to this central interpretation.

Key Fact

AQA assesses unseen poetry across two Assessment Objectives: AO1 (12 marks) — informed personal response with textual references; AO2 (12 marks) — analysis of language, form, and structure. There are no marks for context (AO3) in the unseen section — focus entirely on your own interpretation and analysis of the poet’s methods.

Step 3: Write Your Response

Structure your response in three paragraphs, each analysing a different aspect of the poem. The What-How-Why method works well for each paragraph:

What: Identify a technique or feature the poet uses (e.g. “The poet uses a metaphor comparing memory to water”).

How: Quote the specific words and analyse them closely. What do individual word choices suggest? What sounds, rhythms, or patterns do you notice?

Why: Explain the effect on the reader. How does this technique contribute to the poem’s overall message or mood? This is where your personal interpretation matters most.

Example: The poet presents nature as a powerful but indifferent force. The metaphor “the sea swallowed the shoreline whole” personifies the sea as a predator, with the violent verb “swallowed” suggesting consumption and destruction. The adverb “whole” emphasises the completeness of this erasure — nothing is left. This creates a sense of helplessness in the reader, reinforcing the poem’s message that humanity is insignificant compared to the natural world.

Notice how this paragraph: (1) makes a clear point about the poem’s message, (2) embeds a quotation, (3) analyses specific word choices (“swallowed,” “whole”), (4) identifies a technique (personification, metaphor), and (5) explains the effect on the reader. This is what Level 5-6 analysis looks like.

Common Mistakes

Retelling the poem: The most common mistake is simply describing what happens in the poem. “In the first stanza the poet talks about a bird, then in the second stanza they talk about the sky” — this is summary, not analysis. Always explain the effect of the poet’s choices.

Feature-spotting: Listing techniques without analysing their effect (“The poet uses alliteration, a metaphor, and enjambment”) will not earn high marks. You must explain why the poet chose that technique and what it makes the reader feel or understand.

Ignoring form and structure: Many students only write about language. The examiners specifically reward analysis of form (what type of poem? regular or irregular? rhyme scheme?) and structure (how the poem develops, shifts in tone, the significance of the opening and ending).
exam_tip_html: For Q27 (24 marks), aim for three well-developed paragraphs in 25 minutes. It is better to write three paragraphs with detailed, close analysis of specific words than five paragraphs with surface-level comments. Quality beats quantity. Always refer to the poet as “the poet” — not “the author” or “the writer.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Read the poem three times before writing: first for general meaning, second for themes, third for annotation.
  • Summarise the poem’s message in one sentence before you start writing — this keeps your response focused.
  • Use the What-How-Why structure for each paragraph: identify a technique, quote and analyse the specific words, then explain the effect on the reader.

title: Language & Imagery in Unseen Poetry
description: How to identify and analyse the key language techniques poets use to create meaning, mood, and imagery.
content_html:
Why Language Analysis Matters

AO2 (12 marks) specifically rewards your ability to analyse how poets use language to create effects. This means going beyond naming a technique (“the poet uses a metaphor”) to explaining why that technique works and what it makes the reader feel or understand. The strongest responses zoom in on individual word choices and explore their connotations — the layers of meaning beyond the dictionary definition.

Key Fact

You do not need to identify every technique in a poem. It is far better to analyse two or three techniques in depth than to list ten techniques with no analysis. The examiner wants to see how you think about language, not how many techniques you can name.

Metaphor and Simile

A metaphor states that one thing is another; a simile says one thing is like another. When analysing either, always ask: What qualities are being transferred? If a poet writes “her voice was a knife,” what qualities of a knife are being applied to the voice? Sharpness, the ability to cut, to wound, to penetrate. This is far more useful than simply writing “the poet uses a metaphor.”

Extended metaphors (also called conceits) run through several lines or the whole poem. If you spot an extended metaphor, it is almost certainly the poem’s central idea and should form the basis of your response.

Personification gives human qualities to non-human things. When a poet writes “the wind whispered secrets,” the wind is given the human ability to whisper and have knowledge. Ask: Why does the poet want us to see this object as alive? Usually to make it seem more powerful, more threatening, or more sympathetic.

Pathetic fallacy is a specific type of personification where the weather or landscape reflects the speaker’s emotions. Dark skies for sadness, storms for anger, sunshine for joy. It is one of the easiest techniques to spot and analyse in unseen poetry.

Symbolism is when an object or image represents something beyond itself. A rose might symbolise love; a cage might symbolise imprisonment; a journey might symbolise life. Look for recurring images or objects that seem to carry more significance than their literal meaning.

Sound Devices

Poets choose words partly for how they sound. Sound devices are particularly effective for creating mood and atmosphere, which is a common focus of unseen poetry questions.

Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds. Long vowel sounds (“moaning,” “alone,” “slow”) create a dragging, melancholy mood. Short, sharp vowels (“crack,” “spit,” “hit”) create energy, aggression, or speed.

Sibilance (repetition of “s” sounds) can create a hissing, sinister effect or a soft, soothing whisper, depending on context. Plosives (“b,” “d,” “p,” “t,” “k,” “g”) create harsh, explosive sounds that suggest violence, force, or disruption.

Key Fact

When analysing sound devices, always explain the effect of the sound, not just its presence. “The sibilance in ‘the snake slid silently’ creates a hissing sound that mirrors the snake’s movement, making the reader feel its dangerous, stealthy presence” is analysis. “The poet uses sibilance” is feature-spotting.

Semantic Fields

A semantic field is a group of related words that create a pattern of meaning. If a poem repeatedly uses words like “chains,” “cage,” “locked,” and “trapped,” it has a semantic field of imprisonment, even if it never uses the word “prison.” Identifying semantic fields is one of the most sophisticated skills you can demonstrate, because it shows you are tracking patterns across the whole poem rather than just analysing individual lines.

Step 1: Pick a word that stands out — Look for words that seem surprising, unusual, or emotionally charged. Verbs and adjectives are often the richest for analysis.

Step 2: Consider its connotations — What associations does the word carry? “Crept” connotes stealth, secrecy, fear. “Strode” connotes confidence, power, purpose. The poet chose this word over alternatives — why?

Step 3: Consider its sound — Does the word’s sound contribute to its meaning? “Crash” sounds violent (plosive “cr” + sharp “ash”). “Murmur” sounds gentle (soft “m” sounds).

Step 4: Connect to the poem’s message — How does this word choice contribute to the overall meaning or mood? Always link back to the poet’s purpose.
exam_tip_html: When you find a powerful image or metaphor, spend time on it. The examiner would rather read one paragraph of deep, exploratory analysis than three paragraphs of surface-level comments. Use phrases like “This could suggest” and “Perhaps the poet is implying” to show that you are exploring multiple interpretations — this is exactly what the top mark bands reward.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Always analyse the effect of language techniques, not just their presence. Explain why the poet chose that word or image and what it makes the reader feel.
  • Focus on connotations — the layers of meaning beyond the dictionary definition. This is what separates Level 4-6 responses from Level 1-3.
  • Look for semantic fields (patterns of related words) across the whole poem — they reveal the poet’s central concerns.

glossary_terms.definition: The associated meanings and feelings that a word carries beyond its dictionary definition. For example, 'home' denotes a building but connotes warmth, safety, and belonging.

A direct comparison that states one thing IS another, creating a powerful association between two unlike things. 'Her voice was a knife' compares voice to a weapon, suggesting sharpness and the ability to wound.
A metaphor that is developed and sustained over several lines or throughout an entire poem, creating a detailed parallel between two ideas.
A type of personification in which weather or natural phenomena reflect or mirror the emotions of a character or speaker. Stormy weather during conflict, sunshine during joy.
Repetition of vowel sounds within words in close proximity, creating musicality, harmony, or mood. Long vowels slow the rhythm; short vowels quicken it.
A group of words within a text that relate to the same topic or idea, creating a pattern of meaning.

title: Structure & Form in Unseen Poetry
description: How to analyse the structural and formal choices poets make, including line breaks, stanzas, rhythm, and rhyme.
content_html:
Why Structure and Form Matter

Many students focus exclusively on language when analysing unseen poetry and ignore structure and form entirely. This limits their marks significantly. AO2 explicitly assesses your ability to analyse “the effects of the writer’s methods, using relevant subject terminology: language, form and structure.” The examiner is specifically looking for comments on how the poem is put together, not just what it says.

Key Fact

Form = the overall type or shape of the poem (sonnet, ballad, free verse, monologue, etc.). Structure = how the poem is organised and how it develops (stanza breaks, shifts in tone, the journey from beginning to end, repetition patterns). Both contribute to meaning and should be analysed.

Analysing Form

When looking at an unseen poem, ask: What type of poem is this, and why? Some common forms you might encounter:

Sonnet (14 lines) — traditionally associated with love, but poets often subvert this expectation. If an unseen poem is 14 lines, note this immediately. Ask: is the poet using the sonnet form sincerely or ironically?

Free verse — no regular metre or rhyme scheme. Free verse gives the poet complete control over line breaks and rhythm. If a poem is in free verse, ask: Why has the poet rejected regular form? Usually because the content is irregular, unpredictable, or emotionally raw.

Dramatic monologue — a poem in which a single speaker addresses a silent listener, often revealing more about themselves than they intend. Look for a specific voice, a listener implied by “you,” and details that the speaker might not realise are significant.

Ballad — a narrative poem, often with regular quatrains and a driving ABAB or ABCB rhyme scheme. Ballads tell stories, sometimes with a tragic or moral ending.

Lyric — a short poem expressing personal emotion. Most unseen poems are lyrics. The speaker reflects on feelings, memories, or experiences rather than telling a story.

Analysing Structure

Structure is about how the poem moves from beginning to end. The most useful structural features to analyse are:

The opening: How does the poem begin? An abrupt opening (“Suddenly he awoke”) creates immediacy; a gentle opening (“There once was a country”) creates nostalgia. The first line sets the reader’s expectations — note whether these expectations are fulfilled or subverted.

The ending: How does the poem close? Does it resolve (reaching a conclusion) or remain open (leaving the reader with questions)? A final-line revelation can transform the meaning of everything that came before. Compare the ending with the opening — has the speaker changed?

Key Fact

The volta (turning point) is one of the most important structural features to identify. It is the moment where the poem shifts in tone, direction, or argument. In a sonnet, it traditionally occurs between line 8 and line 9. In other poems, look for words like “but,” “yet,” “however,” or a sudden change in imagery or mood.

Line Breaks, Enjambment, and Caesura

Enjambment is when a sentence continues past the end of a line without punctuation. It creates momentum, breathlessness, or a sense of ideas spilling over. It can also create surprise when the meaning is completed on the next line in an unexpected way.

End-stopped lines end with punctuation, creating pauses and a sense of control or finality. A poem that shifts from enjambment to end-stopped lines might be showing a shift from chaos to calm, or from emotion to reflection.

Caesura (a pause within a line, usually created by punctuation) can create emphasis, break a rhythm, or isolate a word or phrase for impact. A mid-line full stop is particularly dramatic, as it disrupts the flow of the line.

You do not need to identify specific metres in the unseen section, but you should notice whether the poem has a regular or irregular rhythm. A regular rhythm (da-DUM da-DUM) can create a song-like, predictable, or controlled feel. An irregular rhythm can create a sense of disorder, emotion, or natural speech.

Pay attention to changes in rhythm. If a poem has a regular beat that suddenly breaks down, this disruption is significant — it might mirror a shift in emotion, an interruption, or a moment of crisis.

Rhyme creates connections between words and can reinforce meaning. A regular rhyme scheme (ABAB) creates order and predictability; an irregular or broken rhyme scheme can suggest disorder or defiance. Half-rhyme (words that almost but don’t quite rhyme) creates a sense of incompleteness or unease.

Repetition as a Structural Device

Refrains (repeated lines or phrases) create rhythm, emphasis, and a sense of return. Each time a refrain appears, consider whether its meaning has changed because of what has happened since the last repetition. A refrain that means something different at the end of the poem compared to the beginning is a powerful structural technique.
exam_tip_html: Always include at least one point about structure or form in your unseen poetry response. A sentence like “The poet’s shift from regular quatrains to a single isolated final line mirrors the speaker’s move from confidence to isolation” shows the examiner that you can analyse how the poem is constructed, not just what it says. This is what separates Level 4-5 responses from Level 3.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Form is the type of poem (sonnet, free verse, ballad); structure is how the poem develops from beginning to end. Both are assessed under AO2.
  • Look for the volta (turning point), compare the opening and ending, and notice how the poet uses stanza breaks, enjambment, and caesura to control pace and emphasis.
  • Always link structural observations to meaning: explain why the poet chose that form or structure and what effect it creates for the reader.

title: Comparing Two Unseen Poems
description: How to write a focused 8-mark comparison of two unseen poems, linking methods to shared or contrasting themes.
content_html:
The Comparison Task

The unseen comparison asks you to compare the poem you have just analysed with a second unseen poem, focusing on how each poet uses their methods. It carries fewer marks than the longer single-poem analysis that precedes it, so your response should be focused and proportionate — two tight paragraphs are usually enough. The task typically invites you to discuss similarities and/or differences in how the poets present a particular idea or subject. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact timing and wording.

Key Fact

The comparison rewards analysis of methods above all. You must compare the methods (language, structure, form) the poets use, not just the content of the poems. Writing “Both poems are about nature” is content; writing “Both poets use personification to present nature as a living force, but Poet A creates awe while Poet B creates menace” is methods.

Reading the Second Poem

You need to read the second poem quickly and efficiently. Spend a few minutes reading it twice and making brief annotations. Focus on three things:

1. The theme — What is this poem about? How does its subject connect to the first poem?

2. The methods — What techniques stand out? Identify 2-3 methods you can compare with the first poem.

3. Similarities and differences — Comparison tasks usually invite you to discuss both. The strongest responses will consider both, showing how the poets approach the same theme in different ways.

Aim for two focused paragraphs. Each paragraph should compare one specific method used by both poets.

Paragraph 1: A similarity or difference in how the poets use language. Quote from both poems. Analyse the effect of each poet’s word choices and explain how they create similar or contrasting effects.

Paragraph 2: A similarity or difference in how the poets use structure or form. Compare how the poems are organised, how they develop, or how the poets use line breaks, rhythm, or stanza structure to create effects.

Use comparative connectives throughout: “Similarly,” “In contrast,” “Whereas,” “However,” “Both poets,” “While Poet A... Poet B.”

What Markers Reward

Examiner reports consistently point to a clear hierarchy of what moves answers up the bands:

Key Fact

The strongest comparison responses are perceptive and detailed: they compare both poems’ methods throughout, use well-chosen references from both, and offer sophisticated analysis of the effects of language, form and structure. Clearer — but less insightful — work still explains comparisons with relevant references. Weaker work describes the poems separately or attempts only surface-level comparison. The step up is always from describing to analysing effect.

Common Mistakes

Writing about one poem then the other: This is the biggest mistake. Write about both poems in every paragraph. A comparison response that analyses Poem 1 for ten lines and then Poem 2 for ten lines will not access the top band, even if the individual analysis is good.

Comparing content, not methods: “Both poems are about loss” is content. “Both poets use motifs of darkness to represent loss, but Poet A creates quiet sadness while Poet B creates angry despair” is methods. The marks here are entirely for analysis of methods, so this distinction is critical.

Spending too long: This comparison task is shorter than the single-poem analysis that comes before it. Don’t spend more time on the comparison than on the main unseen question. Two focused paragraphs are enough.

Model: Both poets use natural imagery to present the passing of time, but with contrasting effects. In Poem 1, the metaphor “the river carried our laughter to the sea” presents time as a gentle, natural process — the river flows steadily, carrying memories with it. The verb “carried” suggests care and tenderness. In contrast, Poet 2 uses the image of “leaves / torn from the branch by winter’s fist” to present time as violent and destructive. The personification of winter as having a “fist” makes time feel aggressive and forceful, while the enjambment between “leaves” and “torn” mirrors the sudden tearing away. Where Poet 1 accepts time peacefully, Poet 2 resists it with anger.

Useful Comparative Phrases

These phrases will help you compare throughout your paragraphs:

For similarities: “Both poets use [method] to [effect].” “Similarly, Poet 2 employs [technique] to create the same sense of...” “This is echoed in Poem 2, where...”

For differences: “In contrast, Poet 2...” “Whereas Poet 1 uses [method] to create [effect], Poet 2 instead...” “However, the effect in Poem 2 is quite different:...” “Where Poet 1 [approach], Poet 2 [contrasting approach].”
exam_tip_html: Q28 is the last question on the entire paper. Many students rush it or run out of time. To avoid this, keep strict time: 25 minutes for Q27, then 20 minutes for Q28. Two well-developed comparative paragraphs will score higher than four rushed ones. Focus on methods (language, structure, form), not just content — every mark is for AO2.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Q28 is worth 8 marks and is assessed on AO2 only (methods). Compare how the poets use language, structure, and form — not just what the poems are about.
  • Write two focused comparative paragraphs, each discussing both poems together. Never write about one poem and then the other.
  • Use comparative connectives throughout: “Similarly,” “In contrast,” “Whereas,” “Both poets.” These signal to the examiner that you are comparing, not just analysing.

practice_questions.text: In both poems the speakers describe a memory. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present that memory? [In the exam, two poems would be printed.]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive, detailed comparison of both poems' methods. Well-chosen references from both poems. Sophisticated analysis of language, form, and structure.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear, explained comparison with relevant references.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some comparison with some references.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments about one or both poems.

practice_questions.text: In both poems the speakers describe nature. Compare the methods the poets use to present nature.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Compare specific language techniques (e.g. personification, imagery)
• Analyse the effect of each poet's word choices
• Compare structural or formal choices
• Use comparative connectives throughout
• Discuss both similarities AND differences in methods

practice_questions.text: What is the key difference between Q27 and Q28 in terms of what is assessed?
practice_questions.marks:
• Q27 assesses AO1 (personal response, 12 marks) AND AO2 (methods, 12 marks) (1 mark)
• Q28 assesses AO2 ONLY (methods, 8 marks) (1 mark)
• This means Q28 must focus entirely on comparing methods, not content (1 mark)
• Neither question assesses AO3 (context) — no marks for context in unseen poetry (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explain why writing about one poem then the other is a common mistake in Q28.
practice_questions.marks:
• The question asks you to COMPARE, not analyse separately (1 mark)
• A comparison response must discuss both poems in every paragraph (1 mark)
• Writing separately fails to show the examiner that you can compare methods (1 mark)
• The top mark band requires 'detailed comparison' — this means interweaving analysis of both poems (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Write a model comparative paragraph for Q28, comparing how two poets might use personification differently.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): A paragraph that discusses both poems together, using comparative connectives. Quotes from both poems analysed for method and effect. Explores how the same technique (personification) creates different effects in each poem. Precise terminology.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear comparison with relevant examples.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some comparison attempted.
Lower band (1-2): Describes rather than compares.

practice_questions.text: How many paragraphs should you write for Q28 and why?
practice_questions.marks:
• Two well-developed comparative paragraphs (1 mark)
• Each paragraph should compare one specific method used by both poets (1 mark)
• Quality beats quantity — two detailed paragraphs score higher than four rushed ones (1 mark)
• You only have 20 minutes, so two paragraphs is the right balance of depth and time management (1 mark)
